extracted.intended_audience: scientists, research funders, grant reviewers, and policy-makers interested in peer-review fairness
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize findings and implications about how reviewer instructions and interventions affect gender bias in grant peer review — specifically whether reviewers are asked to evaluate the researcher (CV) versus the research (proposal) and the effect of unconscious-bias training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus review on the science (research) rather than the researcher
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask reviewers to assess the research proposal (the science) rather than the applicant's career or CV; doing so makes gender bias 'go away' according to the reported study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that when review criteria emphasize evaluation of the proposed research, female scientists do not suffer the same disadvantage seen when reviewers assess the investigator. Implication: design review forms and instructions to prioritize scientific merit of the proposal to reduce gender disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing the researcher (CV/track record) as a review criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewers are asked to judge the researcher — for example, by weighting the strength of the applicant's CV — women lose out and gender bias is observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating CV/track record as a primary evaluation dimension is presented as an anti-pattern for gender equity in funding decisions. Review panels and funding agencies should be cautious about heavy reliance on applicant career indicators when aiming for equitable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide unconscious-bias training for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Training reviewers to recognize unconscious biases appears to correct gender imbalances in this study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that unconscious-bias training in this context mitigated bias, although it also references earlier work that suggested such training could increase bias, so evidence is mixed. Guidance: consider implementing bias-awareness training alongside careful evaluation-design (e.g., focusing on research) and monitor outcomes, since effectiveness may vary by context and training design.
